claims.claim: Hong Kong should tighten rent control on subdivided units only through second-generation controls that cap increases within tenancies.
The form of rent control matters enormously for whether the policy backfires.
Around 110,000 households live in subdivided units.
SDU tenants pay a premium of 15 to 25 percent per square foot despite lower median rents.
SDU tenants are disproportionately new arrivals, single-parent households, and public housing applicants.
The average public housing wait has hovered around five and a half years.
For SDU tenants the unit is not a choice but a residual option while the queue moves.
High per-square-foot costs, weak bargaining power, and a long housing queue expose tenants to sharp rent hikes.
Standard theory predicts supply contraction under binding rent ceilings.
The long-run elasticity of SDU supply to controlled rent levels is estimated at 0.31 to 0.48.
A 10 percent cap-induced rent reduction removes roughly 3 to 5 percent of SDU stock over five years.
First-generation hard caps on rent levels should not be defended because of supply contraction.
First-generation controls show consistent contraction effects while second-generation controls show small or null effects on stock.
The 2021 Hong Kong ordinance is second-generation and the stable stock in the D2 index is consistent with that.
A cap on increases within a tenancy protects sitting tenants without forcing rent below market.
The estimated 3 to 5 percent stock loss applies to level caps, not within-tenancy caps.
Tightening second-generation rent control targets the risk of a sharp hike while avoiding contraction.
Hong Kong should strengthen within-tenancy increase caps rather than impose hard rent ceilings.

cites.sentence: Around 110,000 households live in subdivided units, and although the median SDU rent is roughly 30 percent below mainstream private flats, tenants pay a premium of 15 to 25 percent per square foot because space is carved up and priced at its most desperate margin [D1p1].
They are disproportionately new arrivals, single-parent households, and residents waiting for public housing, where the average wait has hovered around five and a half years [D1p2].
For these households the SDU is "not a choice but a residual option while the queue moves" [D1p2].

Standard theory predicts supply contraction under binding rent ceilings, and in marginal stock like SDUs the long-run elasticity of supply to controlled rent levels is estimated at 0.31 to 0.48, meaning a 10 percent cap-induced rent reduction removes roughly 3 to 5 percent of stock over five years [D6p1].
First-generation controls, which cap rent levels, show consistent contraction effects; second-generation controls, which cap increases within tenancies, show small or null effects on stock [D6p2].
The 2021 Hong Kong ordinance is second-generation, and the stable stock in the D2 index is consistent with that [D6p2].
The estimated 3 to 5 percent stock loss applies to level caps, not to the within-tenancy approach [D6p1][D6p2].
The estimated 3 to 5 percent stock loss applies to level caps, not to the within-tenancy approach [D6p1][D6p2].

The living conditions and tenant profile show that protection is needed: tenants pay a per-square-foot premium [D1p1], they are the households with the least ability to absorb increases, and they face a five-and-a-half-year wait for public housing [D1p2].

The living conditions and tenant profile show that protection is needed: tenants pay a per-square-foot premium [D1p1], they are the households with the least ability to absorb increases, and they face a five-and-a-half-year wait for public housing [D1p2].

Tightening rent control in the second-generation sense — stronger limits on increases within tenancies — targets the actual vulnerability, which is the risk of a sharp hike, while avoiding the contraction associated with hard caps [D6p2].
The evidence on conditions justifies stronger protection [D1p1][D1p2], and the evidence on supply tells us which kind of protection to choose [D6p1][D6p2].
